You're designing a study of what gives human experience the sense of being or having an I, and what makes that I continue, or seem to. Below are candidate accounts that could inform your study. I haven't evaluated any of them yet.

Mark exactly three as Pursue. Mark each of the rest as Park (worth returning to) or Drop (not worth returning to). Give a one-sentence reason for every item.

A. Contemporary secular mindfulness account of the I as recurrent thought
The sense of being an I is entirely the recurrent thought "I" or "me," which repeatedly attaches itself to sensations, feelings and memories. When attention is turned directly toward it, this thought can be seen to arise and pass like any other, and experience no longer seems organized around a separate owner. The I seems to continue only because the thought recurs so often that the gaps between its appearances go unnoticed.

B. Theravāda Buddhist analysis of I-making and mine-making
What is ordinarily taken to be a person is analyzed into five changing aggregates: bodily form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. None is a self, but through craving and clinging each is repeatedly taken as "this is mine, this I am, this is my self." The sense of being an I comes from this appropriation, including a subtle conceit, "I am," that can persist even after belief in a self is abandoned. The I seems to continue because I-making keeps recurring.

C. Yogācāra Buddhist account of manas and the store-consciousness
Alongside the six forms of sensory and mental awareness runs a largely subliminal store-consciousness, which carries traces of past actions and experiences as seeds that later give rise to new experience. A further mental function, manas, continuously takes this store-consciousness to be a self, accompanied by self-view, self-conceit, self-love and self-delusion. The sense of being an I arises from this constant, largely unnoticed misidentification. The I seems to continue because the store-consciousness flows on like a stream, without ever being a fixed self.

D. Advaita Vedānta account of ahaṃkāra and ātman
Pure consciousness, the witness, is unchanging and is one's true self. The sense of being a particular I, a doer and experiencer with this body and mind, arises through the I-maker, when the witness and the body-mind are mistakenly identified through superimposition. The personal I changes; what truly continues is the unchanging witness with which it is mistakenly identified, present through waking, dreaming and deep sleep.

E. Left-hemisphere interpreter account (drawing on split-brain research)
A system in the brain's left hemisphere, the interpreter, readily generates confident explanations for actions, feelings and bodily states, including ones it did not initiate. On this account the interpreter is the whole source of the self: the sense of being an I is entirely the running explanation it produces to make behavior appear unified and intended. The I seems to continue because the interpreter keeps fitting each new action and feeling into the same explanatory account of who is acting.

F. Phenomenology of the minimal self (Husserl, Zahavi)
The sense of being an I is not constructed on top of experience; it belongs to experience itself. Every conscious experience is given first-personally, as mine, before any reflection, self-concept or story. This pre-reflective self-awareness, or "mineness," is the most basic I. At the most basic, moment-to-moment level, its continuity comes from the temporal structure of consciousness: each present moment retains the just-past and anticipates the about-to-come, so experience is lived as one flow.

G. Narrative self (Dennett, "center of narrative gravity")
People continuously weave their actions, memories and plans into stories, and the I is the protagonist these stories are organized around. Like a center of gravity, it is a useful abstraction rather than a physical part of anything. The sense of being an I arises from this storytelling activity, much of which occurs without deliberate authorship. The I seems to continue because the story is constantly extended and revised so that new events are told as happening to the same character.

H. Predictive processing and self-model theory (drawing on Seth and Metzinger)
The brain continuously predicts the state of its own body, especially internal signals such as heartbeat and breathing, and integrates these predictions into a self-model of the organism. The sense of being an I arises from this self-model, which is transparent: it is not experienced as a model, so the system simply experiences itself as someone. The I seems to continue because relatively stable higher-level expectations about the organism organize changing bodily and perceptual signals over time.
